background: In December 2025, SoundCloud announced it had discovered unauthorised activity on its platform . The incident allowed an attacker to map publicly available SoundCloud profile data to email addresses for approximately 20% of its users. The impacted data included 30M unique email addresses, names, usernames, avatars, follower and following counts and, in some cases, the user’s country.
The attackers later attempted to extort SoundCloud before publicly releasing the data the following month.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
motive: The attackers later attempted to extort SoundCloud before publicly releasing the data the following month.
outcome: 29,815,722 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Avatars, Email addresses, Geographic locations, Names, Profile statistics, Usernames.
editorial: Nothing in this breach was secret. Display names, avatars, follower counts and countries were all public on the platform, and the email addresses were not. The attacker's entire contribution was joining the two, for roughly a fifth of the user base. That join is the product.
A handle chosen precisely because it is not your name is worth very little on its own; attached to a mailbox you actually read, it becomes an identity and a delivery channel at the same time.

Artists who released work under an alias and listeners whose taste they would rather not have attributed to them are in the same file, and no amount of care about what they posted would have kept them out of it, the private half came from the account system, not from anything they published. The practical exposure is phishing with an unusually good hook.

A message quoting your real handle, your follower count and your country reads exactly like the platform, and the platform is precisely who a working musician expects to hear from about payouts, copyright claims and takedowns. Open the app and look; do not follow the link, however specific the message is about a track you genuinely uploaded.

The record says the mapping covered about 20 percent of users, and that is worth checking before assuming you are affected. Not finding your address does not prove your profile was outside the mapped set, because coverage of any breach search depends on the data the service received.

Finding it means the link between your handle and that address is now public, and it will remain so even if you change the email on the account later. The extortion sequence in the record is also familiar: the platform discovered unauthorised activity in December 2025, the attackers attempted to extort SoundCloud, and the data was released publicly the following month.

For creators, the practical step is to separate the address used for the account from any address used for bookings or label contacts, so that a phishing message sent to the leaked address is easier to recognise as such.

fields.name: Geographic locations
fields.why: Where the account was used, which narrows a person down further than most people expect.

fields.name: Names
fields.why: Turns an anonymous address into an identified person, which is what makes targeted phishing possible.

fields.name: Email addresses
fields.why: An exposed address may be used in phishing attempts. Treat unexpected messages with caution.

fields.name: Usernames
fields.why: A matching handle can be a lead to other profiles, but does not prove shared ownership.

fields.name: Avatars
fields.why: Adds detail to a profile that can be assembled from several breaches at once.

fields.name: Profile statistics
fields.why: Adds detail to a profile that can be assembled from several breaches at once.

actions: Be alert to phishing. A message may use details from exposed or collected records to appear familiar; verify requests through the service directly.
breach.scale_line: That is roughly everyone in Australia.
